classification.habitat: Cultivated in dry, sunny agricultural areas; prefers well-drained soils
classification.distribution: Widely cultivated in India and other warm temperate to subtropical regions

identification.description: A small aromatic annual herb with finely divided leaves, small white or pinkish flowers and elongated ridged fruits commonly used as cumin seed.
identification.whole_plant: Slender annual herb, usually less than about half a metre tall.
identification.root: Slender taproot with fine lateral roots.
identification.stem: Erect, slender, branched and grooved stem.
identification.leaf: Alternate, finely dissected, thread-like segments typical of an Apiaceae aromatic herb.
identification.flower: Small flowers arranged in compound umbels, generally white to pale pink.
identification.fruit: Elongated aromatic schizocarp with several longitudinal ridges; the dried fruit is the commercial cumin seed.
identification.seed: Each mericarp contains a single seed; the dried fruit is commonly called cumin seed.
identification.bark: Not applicable as a distinct medicinal bark character.

major_constituents: Fixed oil and other seed metabolites
phytochemistry.chemical_notes: Cumin fruit contains volatile oil; cuminaldehyde is a commonly reported major aroma constituent. Exact composition varies with cultivar, origin and processing.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Cumin is a widely used culinary spice with a long traditional digestive use. Modern studies cover digestive, antioxidant and other effects, but preparation-specific clinical evidence should be assessed separately.
modern_information.safety_notes: Use authenticated food/pharmacopoeial-quality material and avoid inferring therapeutic dosing from culinary amounts.

mnemonics: Jeeraka = cumin fruit: remember the fine leaves, umbels and ridged aromatic fruits.
student.quick_revision: Jeeraka (Cuminum cyminum) is an aromatic Apiaceae annual; the medicinal drug is the dried fruit, and cuminaldehyde is a commonly reported volatile-oil constituent.

teaching_points: Explain why the culinary term 'seed' is botanically treated as fruit/mericarp in Apiaceae.
Demonstrate an aromatic fruit and compound umbel.
discussion_points: Difference between Jeeraka and other Apiaceae fruits
Volatile-oil variation with storage and processing
practical_points: Observe fruit ridges with a hand lens.
Compare aroma, fruit shape and leaf dissection with Dhanyaka.

doctor.quick_reference: Jeeraka — Cuminum cyminum L.; dried fruit is the listed useful part and traditional indications are mainly digestive/Grahani-related.
key_precautions: Use authenticated fruit and appropriate preparation.
Verify dose and formulation from authoritative sources rather than this educational record.
